articles.titleOriginal: An Entirely New Target for Fighting Senescence
articles.summaryOriginal: Researchers have established how a protein that is nearly absent in the literature, PTCHD4, is linked to cellular senescence. Very little previous work In […]

bodyOriginal.text: Researchers have established how a protein that is nearly absent in the literature, PTCHD4, is linked to cellular senescence .

Very little previous work In most papers, after a customary discussion of the mechanics of cellular senescence and current methods of handling it and its repercussions, the researchers go on to discuss previous work relating to the particular approach at hand. However, that does not pertain to this paper; PTCHD4 is only known as being structurally related to PTCH1, which affects the Hedgehog signaling pathway [1]. While some work has linked dysregulation of Hedgehog pathways to accelerated neurodegeneration [2], the specific role of PTCHD4 was not clear.

The researchers found that, when exposed to the genotoxin bleomycin, PTCHD4 increases alongside inflammation markers in a variety of cells, including human fetal lung diploid fibroblasts, mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), alveolar epithelial type II cells (AEC2s), human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and adult retinal pigment epithelial cells. Aging Atlas data confirmed this upregulation in other types of cells as well, and NCBI data listed this molecule as being disease-associated: its presence is negligible under ordinary conditions.

The team then examined young mice, old mice, and progeric mice, staining for PTCHD4 alongside the senescence biomarker p16. The two biomarkers were expressed in similar quantities among each group in multiple tissues. Similar results were found in human tissue samples; idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) patients expressed more PTCHD4 in their lungs than people without the disease, and human lung cells expressing PTCHD4 were more likely to also express established senescence markers.

Significant effects on senescence The next experiment involved creating MEFs that do not express PTCHD4 and then driving them senescent through replication. PTCHD4 was found to be a critical driver of senescence in this group; after an average of eight passages, ordinary MEFs exhibited signs of senescence, such as the key biomarker SA-β-gal, while this did not occur to the PTCHD4-deficient MEFs until an average of passage 14.

This line of experimentation continued with PTCHD4-overexpressing MEFs, which began exhibiting senescence-related features such as SA-β-gal early in passage 5. Similar results were found in AEC2s; the inflammatory biomarkers IL6 and IL8, along with SA-β-gal, were upregulated alongside PTCHD4 overexpression.

This testing continued with live mice. The researchers utilized mice that do not express PTCHD4 along with wild-type mice, and they exposed both groups to D-galactose, which mimics many of the symptoms of natural aging. The mice that did not express PTCHD4 were much more resistant to D-galactose than wild-type mice, and there were no detectable physical or biochemical problems caused by this absence.

The team then continued with naturally aging animals. They found that mice that do not express PTCHD4 naturally live months longer than wild-type mice, and mice without it apparenly do not develop white hair the way that wild-type animals do.

bodyOriginal.alt: PTCHD4 aging

bodyOriginal.text: A further experiment involved subjecting mice to bleomycin, which harms lung function in a way that mimics IPF in people. As expected, the mice exhibited features of lung fibrosis within 21 days. However, the PTCHD4-less mice suffered from fewer symptoms of the disease, retaining more lung capacity, less immune infiltration, less destruction of alveolar tissues, and less fibrosis than wild-type mice.

A well-known signaling pathway In this study, PTCHD4 was found to have no effects on the Hedgehog pathway or related genes. Instead, its effects were found to be due to AKT signaling. AKT activation normally increases with aging, but a lack of PTCHD4 diminished this. The team created MEFs that do not express PTCHD4 but express AKT through a different construct, and these MEFs were not protected by their lack of PTCHD4. Similar experiments involving the direct expression of AKT in other cell types confirmed these results, recapitulating the effects of PTCHD4.

The researchers believe that “PTCHD4 may represent a candidate target for senescence-associated interventions” and that there is “a potential role for PTCHD4 in age-related fibrotic disease.” However, this is an initial study. Further work will need to be done to confirm these results, elucidate the relationship of PTCHD4 and AKT, ascertain any side effects of eliminating or suppressing PTCHD4, and determine if PTCHD4 can be targeted by interventions.

The studio, located in London's vibrant Clerkenwell neighbourhood, aims to showcase the brand's latest workplace research and design solutions in an inspiring physical space.

Steelcase said that the redesigned space now reflects the changing needs of today's workplace, which has been affected by increased screen time, shorter attention span, the rise of AI and a growing wellbeing crisis.

"The new space provides an opportunity to exchange ideas, discover the research and insights shaping the future of work, and experience first-hand how thoughtful design can enhance wellbeing, collaboration and performance."

bodyOriginal.text: A few species of hydra are immortal in their normal environmental conditions, meaning that function does not decline over time and mortality risk does not increase over time. Researchers spent a good deal of time taking care of hundreds of hydra some years ago to demonstrate that this is the case . Hydra are lower animals, essentially a bundle of stem cells capable of regenerating and replacing any part of their bodies, somewhat analogous to an ambulatory embryo. It is an open question as to whether anything we can learn from their biochemistry can be useful in human medicine.

In today's open access paper, researchers report on the employment of telomerase by hydra. Telomeres are repeated sequences at the end of chromosomes that shorten with each cell replication , creating a clock that leads to cell death when telomeres are too short. In most species, somatic cells are limited in this way in order to minimize the risk of cancer, while stem cells employ telomerase to maintain long telomeres while delivering a supply of new daughter somatic cells to replace losses. The body is just a temporary vehicle for an immortal population of germline stem cells, in one view. Hydra are obvious very different in terms of the balance between stem cell behavior versus somatic cell behavior in individuals.
Telomerase expression and activity in the immortal cnidarian Hydra

Most living eumetazoan animals are mortal. A fundamental mechanism underlying cellular and organismal aging in many species is the progressive shortening of telomeres - protective nucleoprotein structures at chromosome ends. The finite replicative lifespan of somatic cells is linked to telomere attrition. The discovery of telomerase, a ribonucleoprotein complex with reverse transcriptase activity that synthesizes telomeric repeats, provided a molecular explanation for the unlimited proliferative potential of germlines, stem cells, and most cancer cells. In humans, telomerase is not expressed in most somatic tissues and is active primarily in germ cells, stem cells, and certain rapidly renewing tissues such as blood or intestinal epithelium .

Comparative studies indicate that telomere dynamics correlate with lifespan, with slower shortening rates in long-lived species. Recent cross-species analyses, however, reveal a more complex picture, suggesting that the relationship between telomere maintenance strategies (telomerase activity vs. alternative lengthening ) and longevity is not strictly deterministic. Nevertheless, it remains a prevailing hypothesis that biologically immortal organisms must possess robust mechanisms for telomere maintenance. Supporting this, sustained telomerase activity in somatic tissues has been documented in non-senescent invertebrate models such as planarians and long-lived bivalves .

Importantly, several taxa , including some hydras, planarians, and rotifers , have been reported to exhibit negligible or undetectable senescence. In this study, we characterized the telomerase of Hydra vulgaris . The expression pattern of the telomerase catalytic subunit (hyTERT) mRNA correlates with regions exhibiting high proliferative potential and remains unchanged during budding or regeneration. These findings were further corroborated by measurements of telomerase activity. Our data suggest that telomerase may play a role in the immortality of Hydra.

articles.titleOriginal: Mattel and BBC Studios Expand Bluey Licensing Partnership
articles.summaryOriginal: The multiyear global partnership brings the Heelers to Barbie, Hot Wheels, Fisher-Price, Polly Pocket, and UNO, with products launching this fall. The post Mattel and BBC Studios Expand Bluey Licensing Partnership appeared first on The Toy Book .

bodyOriginal.text: Mattel and BBC Studios are expanding the world of Bluey through a multiyear global licensing partnership that will bring the animated series to five of Mattel’s franchises. The first products from the collaboration will arrive this fall across Barbie, Hot Wheels, Fisher-Price, Polly Pocket, and UNO.

Created by Joe Brumm and produced by Ludo Studio , Bluey follows a blue heeler dog who lives with her parents, Bandit and Chilli, and younger sister, Bingo. The series is known for its focus on play, family life, humor, and storytelling, and has received multiple Emmy Awards; it was the most-streamed show in the world for two consecutive years, in 2024 and 2025.
“Bluey reminds us that the best play doesn’t require anything extraordinary, just creativity, laughter, and the people you love,” shares Nick Karamanos, Head of Entertainment Partnerships at Mattel .
RELATED BBC Studios Unleashes Global ‘Play the Bluey Way’ Campaign

The collaboration features Bluey characters and stories across Little People figures and playsets, Barbie dolls and accessories, Polly Pocket compact playsets , Hot Wheels vehicles , and UNO card games .
“We’re bringing Bluey, Bingo, and their family and friends to brands fans already know and love, inviting families to create new stories, adventures, and memories together,” Karamanos adds.

The Little People collection includes Bluey, Bingo, Bandit, Chilli, and additional characters, while the Barbie Cutie Reveal line features dolls dressed as Bluey and Bingo characters. Polly Pocket , Hot Wheels , and UNO will each offer their own Bluey-inspired products.

“Bluey has resonated with families around the world because it celebrates the creativity and connection that comes through play,” says Suzy Raia, Executive Vice President, Global Consumer Products at BBC Studios. “Mattel’s portfolio of iconic brands makes them an ideal partner to extend that spirit through new and engaging play experiences.”

The partnership adds Bluey products across five established Mattel franchises as the brand continues to expand its global consumer products program. Bluey makes her feature-film debut in The Bluey Movie next summer, Aug. 6, 2027.
Learn more about Mattel’s portfolio at mattel.com .

articles.summaryOriginal: The Pop Insider is gearing up to celebrate the greatest fans and merch of 2026. The post The Pop Insider Launches Submissions for Second Annual Collectors’ Choice Awards appeared first on The Toy Book .

bodyOriginal.text: The Pop Insider is returning with its second-annual Collectors’ Choice Awards, a program where both fans and industry insiders pick the hottest licensed merch of the year.

The biggest change in this year’s awards program is the introduction of the Fan Awards, highlighting cosplayers, fans, and collectors who have stood out in their fandoms and communities over the past year. For only $10, fans can nominate themselves or others to be recognized for these awards.
There are five fan categories open for submission, including:
Cosplayer of the Year (highlights a cosplayer who has made an impact on their fandom and community)
Cosplay Group of the Year (highlights a cosplay group that has made an impact on their fandom and community)
Fan of the Year (highlights a non-cosplayer fan who has made an impact on their fandom and community)
Fan Group of the Year (highlights a non-cosplayer fan group that has made an impact on their fandom and community)
Collector of the Year (highlights a fan with an expansive and iconic collection)

Nominations for The Collectors’ Choice Awards are also available now to manufacturers, retailers, publicists, designers, marketing agents, and more. Finalists will be named at the beginning of the new year in 2027, with fans voting on their favorite finalists in January and February. Winners will be announced in March.
There are 20 industry categories open for submission, including:
Best Overall Collectible Line (Action figures, statues, replicas, and more!)
Best High-End Collectible (premium figures, statues, replicas valued at $200+)
Best Action Figure Line (1:6-scale figures, 3.75-inch scale figures, and more)
Best Individual Collectible (highlights collectibles that aren’t a part of a specific lineup)
Best Blind Box Collection (highlights mystery boxes and surprise toys)
Best Prop Replica (collectibles based on props and other items from a franchise)
Best Apparel Collection (capsule collections, licensed apparel)
Best Home Goods Line (kitchenware, decor, furniture, etc.)
Best Tabletop Gaming Collab (board games, tabletop accessories)
Best Fandom Collab (a crossover or unique licensing deal that created must-have merch)
Best Accessory Line (jewelry, watches, bags, etc.)
Best Con Exclusive (limited to SDCC, NYCC, and other con-exclusive collectibles)
Best Limited-Edition Drop (collectibles produced in a quantity of 1,000 or fewer)
Best Branded Experience (permanent installation, interactive experience, or limited activation featuring a brand or IP)
Licensing Program of the Year (licensors)
Retailer of the Year (highlights a key fandom merch destination)
The Underdog Award (highlighting small businesses and industry members who make a difference)
Breakout Hit of the Year (highlights the up-and-coming brands and collectibles that hit the scene)
Designer of the Year (recognizing designers behind the merch)
Nominations for the Collectors’ Choice Awards are open from now until Oct. 30. For more information, click here .

articles.titleOriginal: HappyKids and MLB Partner to Bring MLB Clubhouse to Families
articles.summaryOriginal: The partnership brings animated, educational programming to the streaming platform. The post HappyKids and MLB Partner to Bring MLB Clubhouse to Families appeared first on The Toy Book .

bodyOriginal.text: HappyKids and Major League Baseball (MLB) are partnering to bring MLB Clubhouse , MLB’s youth-focused digital content platform, to HappyKids audiences.

The partnership marks HappyKids’ first collaboration with a major sports league and adds a slate of MLB programming to the free, ad-supported streaming platform. The content includes original animated series, behind-the-scenes player features, game highlights, and creative and educational programming designed to introduce baseball and softball to young fans.

“Reaching young fans means meeting them on the platforms where they already spend their time with their families,” explains Gregg Klayman, Senior Vice President, Product Development and Content Strategy, MLB . “Partnering with HappyKids allows us to put MLB Clubhouse in front of families in a trusted, co-viewing environment, extending the reach of our content well beyond our own channels and helping more households discover the fun, creativity, and personalities that make baseball and softball unique.”

MLB Clubhouse content began rolling out on HappyKids last month, with additional programming planned on an ongoing basis. The content is available through happykids.tv and the HappyKids apps on Roku, Fire TV, Samsung Plus TV, Vizio, LG, and other major streaming devices.
The partnership comes as HappyKids reports that 85% of viewing on the platform is driven by family co-viewing and that the service generates more than 800 million monthly impressions.

“HappyKids’ goal has always been to meet the demand of our audience and bring them the content they are looking to watch,” shares David Di Lorenzo, Senior Vice President, Content Acquisitions and Partnerships, Future Today.
The deal also marks a broader push into sports content for HappyKids, which plans to pursue additional partnerships with major sports leagues in the coming months.

bodyOriginal.text: After years of helping companies get their toys onto retail shelves, Traverse Group is taking the next step and developing a product portfolio of its own.

The retail group has launched ToyVerse, a new toy company making its industry debut at the LA Fall Preview 2026 . This venture will develop both original and licensed products across a wide range of categories — including construction, novelty, plush, crafts, and collectibles — all brought to market by Traverse Group’s well-established supply chain and retail infrastructure. The first toys will begin rolling out to retailers in Fall 2027.
Traverse Group is entering the toy development game with ToyVerse. | Source: Traverse Group

“Launching our own toy development company was a natural progression given the retail reach and customer base the Traverse team has built up over the years,” said JD Hayes, co-founder of Traverse Group. “We are excited to build on our strong retail footprint and leverage our end-to-end supply chain infrastructure to bring innovative products directly to consumers worldwide.”

Leading the operation is industry legend Claire Carroll, who joins ToyVerse from multiple senior leadership roles at Toy Monster and Moose Toys . She will oversee the venture from its newly created headquarters in Melbourne, Australia.

articles.titleOriginal: Asymptomatic Persistent Infection as a Contribution to Degenerative Aging
articles.summaryOriginal: Persistent infections such as cytomegalovirus and other herpesviruses most likely accelerate aging, primarily via harmful effects on the immune system that lead to earlier immunosenescence and chronic inflammation than would otherwise be the case. A range of mechanistic and epidemiological research broadly supports this hypothesis. It remains challenging to completely clear persistent viral infect

bodyOriginal.text: Persistent infections such as cytomegalovirus and other herpesviruses most likely accelerate aging, primarily via harmful effects on the immune system that lead to earlier immunosenescence and chronic inflammation than would otherwise be the case. A range of mechanistic and epidemiological research broadly supports this hypothesis. It remains challenging to completely clear persistent viral infections, however. If a strong antiviral therapy existed , epidemiological data would likely prove the point one way or another within five to ten years, as effects on aging would become apparent in older populations. As it stands, the present relatively weak antiviral therapies show some evidence for positive effects on late life risk of mortality and age-related disease, but not in all studies.

Asymptomatic infections are traditionally considered harmless, reflecting effective immune control and the absence of clinical disease. Yet growing evidence shows that these silent encounters with microbes are far from being immunologically neutral. Throughout life, humans are challenged by a remarkably broad spectrum of viruses and bacteria, including latent pathogens that persist, fluctuate, or periodically reactivate without producing significant symptoms. From an evolutionary standpoint, this represents a fundamental trade-off. Long-lived hosts benefit from maintaining diverse commensal , latent, and low-grade persistent microbes that enhance immune readiness, promote cross-protective immunity , and reduce vulnerability to severe infections. However, this adaptive advantage is counterbalanced by the continuous burden of chronic, almost undetectable immune activation and inflammation, and by the energetic cost of sustaining such mechanisms of surveillance.

In this regard, retroviral integrations provide a striking illustration of how persistent viral presence has shaped the evolution of complex organisms by introducing new regulatory elements , immune modulators, and developmental programs. These ancient viral imprints demonstrate that clinically-silent host-microbe interactions can exert long-term selective pressures and influence species-specific biological trajectories. At the individual level, repeated asymptomatic infections trigger transient waves of immune activation, endothelial perturbation, mitochondrial stress, and complement engagement. Although each episode is mild and self-limited, their cumulative burden generates micro-damage that accelerates immunosenescence, perturbs metabolic and vascular homeostasis , and contributes to the progressive rise in systemic inflammation characteristic of aging.
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.arr.2026.103340

articles.titleOriginal: P2RX7 Antagonism Reduces Macrophage Senescence in the Aging Kidney
articles.summaryOriginal: Cells become senescent constantly throughout life in response to various forms of damage and stress, ceasing replication and generating a potent mix of inflammatory signals. In youth, these cells are promptly cleared by the immune system, but with advancing age they begin to linger and accumulate. The inflammatory signaling becomes disruptive to tissue structure and function when sustained over th

bodyOriginal.text: Cells become senescent constantly throughout life in response to various forms of damage and stress, ceasing replication and generating a potent mix of inflammatory signals. In youth, these cells are promptly cleared by the immune system , but with advancing age they begin to linger and accumulate. The inflammatory signaling becomes disruptive to tissue structure and function when sustained over the long term, and this is an important contribution to degenerative aging. Here, researchers show that macrophage cells in the kidney express increasing amounts of the P2RX7 receptor on the cell surface as they progress towards becoming senescent, and blocking this receptor with a suitable antagonist small molecule reduces macrophage senescence and improves kidney function.

Macrophage senescence is a pathological feature in aging or diseased kidneys. However, the role of senescent macrophages in kidney injury and aging has not been fully elucidated yet. We integrated the analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing datasets and the adoptively transfusion of pretreated bone marrow-derived macrophages to investigate the role of renal macrophage senescence in kidney injury. Here, we portrayed the senescence trajectory along multiple time points in infiltrating macrophages, and observed the persistent increase of macrophage-expressed purinergic receptor P2RX7 along the senescence trajectory in injured kidneys of septic mice.

Importantly, our discovered small-molecule P2RX7 antagonist strikingly improved kidney function and pathological damage, as well as mitigated macrophage senescence in septic and aging mice. Mechanistically, P2RX7 antagonist could promote the wound healing , migration , and proliferation capacity of senescent reparative macrophages, thus exerting anti-inflammatory effects and repairing kidney tissues. Together, our findings illustrate the crucial participation of senescent macrophages in septic kidney injury, and offer novel therapeutic strategy via intervening P2RX7 against immunosenescence -associated kidney injury and aging.
Link: https://doi.org/10.7150/ijbs.138299

articles.titleOriginal: London has "the best architecture and interior design community in Europe" says Duncan Riches
articles.summaryOriginal: As Shoreditch Design Week kicks off its inaugural edition at this year's London Design Festival, we interviewed creative director Duncan Riches about how he aims to bring design back to the east London neighbourhood. If you ask people in London's design scene which of the ever-increasing London Design Festival (LDF) districts are a must-visit, chances The post London has "the best architecture and

bodyOriginal.text: As Shoreditch Design Week kicks off its inaugural edition at this year's London Design Festival , we interviewed creative director Duncan Riches about how he aims to bring design back to the east London neighbourhood.

If you ask people in London's design scene which of the ever-increasing London Design Festival (LDF) districts are a must-visit, chances are they'll say Brompton – where the V&A hub is – and Shoreditch.

The ex-industrial east London neighbourhood was the epicentre of the city's creative scene during the early 2000s, but has since become better known for its restaurants and nightlife – which seem to cater mostly to tourists – than its independent designers.

That could be about to change, though, as Riches, creative director of the newly minted Shoreditch Design Week , aims to help emerging designers and commercial brands work together to bring the design trade back to Shoreditch.

The week will be centred around four curated trade exhibitions, including the interior design show House of Icon at Shoreditch Town Hall, graduate design showcase New Designers and materials fair Material Matters .

"I want to have a real core of trade; brands that show in the main venues, people from across London, hopefully companies from across the UK, and even better, companies not from the UK who want to work in the UK," Riches told Dezeen.
"I want to get those brands with their products in front of our audience – honestly, we have the best architecture and interior design community in the whole of Europe."

bodyOriginal.alt: Portrait of Duncan Riches

bodyOriginal.text: Duncan Riches is the creative director for Shoreditch Design Week. Photo by Luciana Britton Newell As well as the larger exhibitions, the week will also feature numerous smaller shows, while local brands such as Ally Capellino and Lee Broom will open up their showrooms to the public for product launches and drinks.

Riches's aim is for Shoreditch Design Week to become a place where "all the young talent and the emerging things can also have a home because really, what they all need is footfall and professional interest".
Shoreditch hospitality doesn't "have a relationship with the daytime economy"

But making Shoreditch fertile ground for designers once again is not without its challenges. Other popular design weeks, perhaps especially Copenhagen's 3 Days of Design , often integrate the entire neighbourhood, something that doesn't currently happen in Shoreditch.
"One of the problems in Shoreditch is there are so many restaurants and bars and a nighttime economy," Riches said.

"They don't have a relationship with the daytime economy. If you go to 3 Days, you'll go to a lovely showroom, you'll see some beautiful lights, and then the florist across the road has got the lights hanging there and the pastries are from the pastry shop next door."

Read: London design "an international success story" says Sadiq Khan In contrast, Shoreditch doesn't have those connections as the industries aren't working together, according to Riches, despite his various attempts to integrate them.
"I desperately tried to get a lovely restaurant last year to take out all of their furniture and put in Fredericia because they wanted to do a show there," he said.
"They were like, 'You're mad. What is this?' And then like four weeks before, they said, 'Oh, we think we could do that.' And I said, 'We need to know four months in advance."

With events company Media 10 having recently bought Shoreditch Design Week – formerly known as Shoreditch Design Triangle – from furniture brand SCP , Riches says the event now has access to larger spaces and is able to put on much bigger shows.

"What Media 10 do, and the investment that they bring, is multi-year deals," he said. "So when you go to Shoreditch Town Hall and say to them, 'Look, we want to do it for three years,' you get the kind of rate which allows you to put on a show and make it okay in terms of the cost for the exhibitors."
Riches believes there is still a need for an event that is more focused on people working in the industry – something that he thinks is lacking when it comes to LDF as a whole.

"They've done a brilliant job in promoting design culture across London," he said. "But what happened is they've stopped serving the kind of core design community, and that is furniture, product, lighting, textiles, ceramics, glass – that kind of world."

"It's great that there's a platform for design, all types of design around London. But the people in the industry, they need an industry event; they need buyers to come, they need architects to come. They need both of them."

bodyOriginal.alt: Installation at London Design Festival

bodyOriginal.text: Prima Material will show Demolition to Design at Material Matters in Shoreditch. Photo by Tom Carter Riches believes that creating a trade hub in Shoreditch will also prove to be beneficial for the wider LDF event.
"I just hope that us being able to create a kind of trade epicentre, if you like, will really help LDF in general," he said.
And while he doesn't see Shoreditch Design Week as being a competitor to LDF, Riches also wants the area to have its own unique identity.
"We've called it 'Design Week', by the way," he said, "because it really does need to stand on its own two feet."

Riches hopes the mixed programme at this year's inaugural edition will mean that everyone can see something they're interested in – whether it's design industry people spending a whole day in the area, or people who just swing by an event after work.
As well as the main flagship shows, there are a number of younger designers showcasing their work, including design gallery Slancha .
Riches sees facilitating collaborations between smaller designers and brands – such as Slancha 's takeover of the shop at The Hoxton hotel this year – as a key part of his job.

"My role is to be a friend to everyone," he said. "Often brands are so wrapped up in the busyness of what they're doing, they find it hard to actually know who to go to or where to go. My job is like a massive matchmaker."

But there might be less need for design matchmaking in the future. Riches has found that emerging designers today are more capable of getting their work seen than in previous years, which he takes as a reassuring sign.

Read: Five galleries injecting renewed energy into the London design scene "If I take a young designer now and I look at their knowledge base, I think they're a lot more canny than they were 15 years ago," he said.
Overall, he believes that the current London design scene is also more vibrant than it has been in many years.
"There is loads to be really positive about right now, and I'm just amazed at where we're at," said Riches.

"And as a Londoner, I'm just kind of thrilled to come back, because London always has that up and down. It's always going to have that, but it feels like we're at the stage where it's just coming up once again, and there's a bit more excitement about it."
The main image of House of Icon in 2025 is by Sam Frost.
This article was originally written as part of our Dezeen Dispatch magazine for LDF 2026. Read an online version of the magazine here .

Shoreditch Design Week runs from 15 to 20 September. See our London Design Festival 2026 guide on Dezeen Events Guide for information about the many other exhibitions, installations and talks that take place during the week.

articles.summaryOriginal: Designer Lee Broom has created an "atmospheric environment" in his Shoreditch showroom with The Chant Chambers, an installation showcasing his glass-block Chant lighting collection at London Design Festival. The Chant Chambers displays the modular light in a variety of forms – as a portable lamp, wall lamp, linear pendants and oversized chandeliers. All are presented inside The post Lee Broom evok

bodyOriginal.text: Designer Lee Broom has created an "atmospheric environment" in his Shoreditch showroom with The Chant Chambers, an installation showcasing his glass-block Chant lighting collection at London Design Festival .
The Chant Chambers displays the modular light in a variety of forms – as a portable lamp, wall lamp, linear pendants and oversized chandeliers.

bodyOriginal.alt: Sculpture in showroom

bodyOriginal.text: Lee Broom added plinths and sculptures to his showroom All are presented inside Broom 's showroom, where textured vertical screens create a series of interconnected spaces designed to have a cinematic atmosphere.
The Chant Chambers, which Broom described as "an elegant yet surreal lounge," has wood-panelled walls and tactile wall-to-wall carpeting and features stone plinths and a number of sculptures.

bodyOriginal.alt: Inside of Chant Chambers

bodyOriginal.text: Wood panels and textured screens divide the space "I wanted the Chant Chambers to feel like an atmospheric environment rather than a display of individual lights," Broom told Dezeen.
"The installation explores how the same cubic form can be transformed as it is repeated across a space, using different configurations to create a sense of discovery," he continued.
"It also reflects the way our clients are looking for lighting that can be adapted specifically to their interiors rather than choosing a single fixed object."

bodyOriginal.alt: Zig-zagging ceiling lights

bodyOriginal.text: Glass-cube pendants were hung in lines to create an architectural feel Broom also used Chant lights in linear arrangements as geometric ceiling designs with an architectural feel.
The moody, smoky colour palette of the installation was inspired by Chant's latest iteration – a smoked-glass finish in a darker tone than the previous design.

Read: Lee Broom displays "sculptural tableau of light" for Mexico City art week debut "The new smoked glass finish was a starting point for the concept," Broom said. "It has a depth and warmth that works particularly well with the design of Chant and it nods to the late 1970s, early 80s period when glass blocks were very prevalent in modern architecture."
"The palette was developed around those darker, richer tones to create a space that feels alluring and atmospheric, while still allowing the geometry of the lighting to stand out," he continued.

bodyOriginal.alt: Artwork and cube lamp

bodyOriginal.text: Broom drew on 1970s interiors for the installation Glamorous 1970s interiors have been making a comeback, with a number of designers looking to the decade for their interiors, as seen recently in a Marseille wine bar .
Broom believes that his Chant light has played a part in this trend, especially when it comes to bringing geometric forms and glass blocks back into contemporary interiors.
"Since I first introduced the original Chant Chandelier in 2022, those references have gained real momentum," he said.
"What interests me is reinterpreting them rather than simply recreating the 1970s, giving those nostalgic materials a more contemporary expression."

bodyOriginal.alt: The Chant Chambers installation

bodyOriginal.text: Wall sconces also decorate the space He argues that these types of interiors also help put the focus on the lighting.
"This kind of aesthetic really allows lighting to take centre stage, not just through the fixtures themselves, but through the ambience they create," Broom said.
At the end of The Chant Chambers installation, Broom placed a three-tier Chant chandelier to fully showcase the lighting collection.

bodyOriginal.alt: Chandelier in London showroom

bodyOriginal.text: A three-tiered chandelier completes the installation The designer has previously created a "sculptural tableau of light" for Mexico Design Week and a chandelier installation for last year's London Design Festival .

The Chant Chamber is on show at 95 Rivington Street, EC2A 3AY, from 15 to 20 September. See our London Design Festival 2026 guide on Dezeen Events Guide for information about the many other exhibitions, installations and talks that take place during the week.

articles.titleOriginal: What this elegant redesign of a sparkling water brand teaches us about packaging in 2026
articles.summaryOriginal: Antwerp studio WeWantMore's refresh of BRU trades a second-long shelf glance for a seat at the table. It's become such a cliché in packaging design, you'd think it was law. Everything needs to be opti...

bodyOriginal.text: Antwerp studio WeWantMore's refresh of BRU trades a second-long shelf glance for a seat at the table.

It's become such a cliché in packaging design, you'd think it was law. Everything needs to be optimised for that single second a shopper glances at it on a shelf. It needs to stand out from the crowd, lure people in. You only have the time it takes for a heart to beat, so don't waste it. Throw everything you have into drawing the eye.

All of which makes a lot of sense. But it's useful to remember that not every single product is fighting for attention from tired and time-poor supermarket shoppers. Sometimes, packaging needs to do very different things.

Sparkling water is a great example. Many of us go to the supermarket for the low-cost stuff, where we expect them to pile it high and sell it cheap. But when we're in a restaurant, the design of a bottle—whether it's wine or water—is an important part of the experience.
In short, we want something to visually elevate our evening out. And that's something Belgian sparkling water brand BRU, which has long been associated with fine dining, understood well.

Who is BRU? BRU can trace its origins back to the 17th century, when it started bottling the natural spring water of Stoumont, in the Ardennes. In modern times, it's been commercialised as a table water brand through the Spadel group, with a name shortened from the French word bruisser (meaning to rustle or murmur).

bodyOriginal.alt: Three framed vintage-style BRU sparkling water posters and advertisements displayed on a wood-panelled wall above a formally set dining table with white tablecloths and glassware
Blue awning above a restaurant entrance featuring BRU branding and "Some things just belong on the table" tagline, with elegant wooden doors and stone facade behind

bodyOriginal.text: What is stylish and sophisticated at one time, though, can be perceived as old-hat and boring a few decades on. And in recent years, however, BRU had become increasingly perceived in this way.

WeWantMore , a creative agency founded in Antwerp in 2006, set out to change that, repositioning it "from a restaurant staple to the finishing touch for the table, designed for every meaningful moment shared around food." An important aspect of that was shifting the focus of the packaging from trying to stand out in the shop to being something people would be proud to display on their table.

Calm and disciplined The new packaging does a great job of putting that idea into practice. The tone is calmer, with a colour palette centred around a deep navy blue that both feels refined and evokes obvious associations with water.

bodyOriginal.alt: Clear glass bottle of BRU sparkling water with blue label featuring a deer motif and blue screw cap, casting a soft shadow against a cream background
Bottle of BRU sparkling water with a redesigned label featuring a blue leaping stag and bold typography against a white background
Three bottles of BRU sparkling water with white labels featuring a navy deer logo and typography, displayed against a neutral background

bodyOriginal.text: The existing brand emblem of a leaping stag is now sleek and sculptural, while avoiding the "minimise everything down to nothing" trend that might have robbed it of all its distinctiveness. And while the lettering is colourful and decorative, it never overwhelms the label, thanks to a disciplined approach to the use of white space.

The result is a design that delivers exactly what WeWantMore set out to achieve. A bottle that people would actively want in front of them while eating, and a brand slogan, "Some things just belong on the table", to drive it all home.

Key takeaways For designers in general, I'd say there are a couple of key takeaways from this story. Firstly, don't ever assume what your design needs to do. It might seem obvious to you that something, for example, needs to stand out on the shelves, but maybe it doesn't. Maybe it won't even appear on the shelves at all.

bodyOriginal.alt: La Touche Perlée logo in white typography on a deep blue background
Bright blue sculptural stag with branching antlers in a leaping pose against a cream background
Person holding a BRU sparkling water brand card displaying the logo and tagline "Naturally sparkling, some things just belong on the table

bodyOriginal.text: Yes, we all want to dive into making cool things as soon as possible. But before you open that Photoshop document, before you start brainstorming even, you need to be absolutely sure you understand the product, the business behind it, the target audience.

The second lesson, I think, is that heritage is an asset to treasure, but rarely needs to be preserved in aspic. WeWantMore could have kept its stag exactly as it was, or completely ditched it; both approaches would probably have been disastrous.

Instead, they subtly modernised it in a way that didn't alienate fans, but would also attract new ones. That's never an easy task, but if you pull it off as a designer, the world will soon be beating a path to your door.

bodyOriginal.text: Not A Hotel has announced it will open a guest room shaped like a giant Poké Ball Designed by Not A Hotel 's in-house team of architects, the structure will comprise two moulded acrylic hemispheres and a curved acrylic window, giving the appearance of an opening ball.

The post Herman Mill

bodyOriginal.text: Promotion: American furniture design brand Herman Miller has been honing its Aeron office chair for decades, equipping it with innovative materials and features for modern workplaces.
Featuring an ergonomic form that supports sitters of different sizes and technological enhancements for better long-term sitting, Aeron was first designed in 1994 by Bill Stumpf and Don Chadwick.

According to Herman Miller , its launch was revolutionary in the office furniture industry, and it continues to lead the charge, thanks to a timeless design informed by ongoing research and use of innovative materials.

bodyOriginal.alt: Aeron office chair by Herman Miller

bodyOriginal.text: The chair was originally designed in 1994 "For decades, we've been perfecting it so that it's not only good for your body, but good for our environment too," says MillerKnoll vice president of sustainability, Gabe Wing.
"Aeron's launch was revolutionary in the office furniture industry, and it continues to lead the charge thanks to updated research, material innovation, and an iconic design that lasts."

bodyOriginal.alt: Aeron office chair by Herman Miller

bodyOriginal.text: Aeron is intended to be used in both home offices and workplaces The most recent iteration of Aeron is equipped with Herman Miller's patented 8Z Pellicle, an elastomeric suspension material designed to assist weight distribution. It features an adjustable back support system that helps encourage a healthy posture when sitting.
The chair's tilting motions also mirror the sitter's natural pivot points at the joints, moving with the body to help keep it relaxed.

bodyOriginal.alt: Office seating by Herman Miller

bodyOriginal.text: It has been fine-tuned to be comfortable for all body types Over 50 per cent of Aeron is constructed from recycled materials, including ocean-bound plastic waste, which Herman Miller has been incorporating into the design since 2021.
The ergonomic office chair comes in three sizes and is available in six colours that range from dark blacks and blues to varying tones of grey and an olive green.

bodyOriginal.alt: Office seating by Herman Miller

bodyOriginal.text: Users can select from a curated range of colourways and finishes "Aeron's material innovation is at the heart of its sustainability story, and a lesson in the major effects of dematerialisation," says Wing.

"Not only is Aeron actively innovated upon, but it's also naturally sustainable through its quality design, which keeps it out of landfills. When we say Aeron is a lasting design, we mean it wholeheartedly."

articles.titleOriginal: Peanuts Expands Across EMEA and APAC
articles.summaryOriginal: WildBrain CPLG has brokered new collaborations spanning multiple categories and location-based entertainment. The post Peanuts Expands Across EMEA and APAC appeared first on The Toy Book .

bodyOriginal.text: Peanuts is expanding its consumer products and experiential presence across the U.K., Europe, the Middle East and Africa ( EMEA ), and Asia-Pacific ( APAC ), building on the momentum of its 75th anniversary year.

Brokered by WildBrain CPLG , the new program spans fashion, accessories, homeware, gifting, health and beauty, food and beverage, family entertainment , and more. The expansion includes collaborations with established brands, retailers, and location-based entertainment partners.

“Peanuts continues to grow as a global fashion and lifestyle brand with premium collaborations, elevated design partnerships, and strong retail momentum,” says Pau Pascual, Senior Vice President Commercial, the U.K., Europe and the Americas, WildBrain CPLG . “With a unique ability to transcend generations and cultures, Peanuts continues to find new and meaningful ways for fans to wear, collect, and share their favorite characters.”

In fashion and accessories, Tommy Hilfiger has launched a children’s apparel and accessories collection, available globally except in the U.S., while Thomas Sabo has introduced a new summer charm collection. In the U.K., Lazy Oaf has launched a second capsule collection focused on Snoopy’s brother Olaf, Primark is expanding its Peanuts offerings across apparel, homewear, and accessories, and Chinti & Parker has introduced a summer fruit-themed collection. Anya Hindmarch has also launched a space-themed Peanuts accessories collection following its Beagle Scouts-inspired line, with a dedicated London pop-up scheduled for October.

Across Europe and APAC, new offerings include apparel from Arket, homeware from Rice, collectible brass figurines from Skultuna, gifting products from Pluto Design, and a new collection from Happy Socks coming in October. Additional collaborations span apparel, accessories, plush , housewares, electronics, and other categories.

The program also includes a range of regional partnerships. Melodi Chocolate has launched a Peanuts chocolate collection in Türkiye, while Lark International has partnered with Popeyes on a promotion featuring six collectible Snoopy charms. Mayoral and Hydroponic have introduced infant apparel and beach- and surf-inspired apparel and skate accessories in Spain, respectively, while Fritzi has launched bags in Germany, and Essentiel Antwerp has introduced an apparel, accessories, and jewelry capsule in Benelux.

In France, Monoprix is partnering with Peanuts on a children’s capsule for the first time, while Galeries Lafayette’s Cadet Rousselle will launch a Fall/Winter 2026 apparel collection for babies and kids. Lexibook will introduce a range of electronic toys and games, including nightlights, alarm clocks, educational laptops, walkie-talkies, headphones, and digital watches, while Jemini will launch plush, homeware, and furniture.

APAC collaborations include women’s apparel from South Korean label Farven, an infant collection from 29CM and Echond, streetwear from JKND and thisisneverthat, and trend-focused apparel for teenage girls from 1Jinn in China. In Taiwan, health and beauty brand Moody has introduced products featuring Snoopy and Olaf.
RELATED EXCLUSIVE: WildBrain Heads to Annecy with First Look at Strawberry Shortcake and Peanuts

Peanuts is also expanding its retail and cultural activations across APAC. Recent and ongoing experiences include the Peanuts gang at South Korea’s Starfield Balloon Festival, a Snoopy Garden pop-up at Jeju Airport, and a Valentine’s Day promotion at CU stores in South Korea. At Singapore’s Changi Airport, a Snoopy and His Siblings pop-up brought the wider Peanuts cast to Terminal 3.

In Indonesia , PT Provaliant Premium Cemerlang hosted a 54-day Many Faces of Snoopy experience at Pantai Indah Kapuk featuring a Peanuts pop-up store, immersive installations, character appearances, and family activities. The activation concluded with a Snoopy Run last week that attracted approximately 6,000 runners and 600 dogs.

Additional activations are underway in China and Taiwan, including a Momibook marketing activation and pop-up store on Wukang Road, the Dream Maker Snoopy: Age of Voyage event at Chengdu IFS, a Snoopy and His Siblings-themed weekend with Taiwan’s CTBC Brothers baseball team, and Peanuts-themed installations and pop-ups in Taichung.

Upcoming Taiwan activations include a Halloween takeover in Taoyuan in October, a year-long pickleball partnership featuring a Snoopy-themed court, themed displays at Taipei 101, and a 600-drone show scheduled for Dec. 3. In Thailand, Peanuts has partnered with Makro and Lotus on an activation featuring large-scale inflatables and a dedicated product offering.

The brand is also expanding its location-based entertainment footprint. In China, the Snoopy & Friends Family Entertainment Center at Magic World offers an immersive, space-exploration-themed destination featuring Snoopy , Woodstock, and the Peanuts gang. In South Korea, the How Do You Do, Snoopy? exhibition from Blue Dragon Art has launched following stops across the Asia-Pacific.

“Peanuts continues to resonate so powerfully because each generation discovers something personal in these characters and their stories,” shares Lisa Silverman Meyers, Senior Vice President, International Licensing & Partnerships, Peanuts Worldwide. “The breadth and creativity of these collaborations across EMEA and APAC demonstrate how Peanuts can feel both timeless and completely relevant to audiences today.”

The new initiatives follow the introduction of new Peanuts content produced by Peanuts and WildBrain , which is rolling out on Apple TV. The Peanuts Featuring brand initiative is also highlighting different groups of characters through rotating themes, including the aforementioned Snoopy and His Siblings, The Girls, and Woodstock and Friends.
WildBrain CPLG is showcasing Peanuts licensing and location-based entertainment opportunities for EMEA and APAC at Brand Licensing Europe at stand B171.

articles.titleOriginal: Midlife Growth Hormone Receptor Ablation Modestly Slows Aging in Mice
articles.summaryOriginal: Despite considerable and growing effort put towards the development of novel means to slow and reverse aging over the past thirty years, the longest lived laboratory mice remain those lineages first established in the 1990s with mutations that disable growth hormone metabolism, such as via knockout of growth hormone or growth hormone receptor genes. These mice are small and vulnerable to cold, but

bodyOriginal.text: Despite considerable and growing effort put towards the development of novel means to slow and reverse aging over the past thirty years, the longest lived laboratory mice remain those lineages first established in the 1990s with mutations that disable growth hormone metabolism , such as via knockout of growth hormone or growth hormone receptor genes. These mice are small and vulnerable to cold, but live as much as 70% longer than their unmodified peers.

It seems likely that this has little relevance to human aging, as Laron syndrome is the analogous human inherited condition, usually caused by a growth hormone receptor loss of function mutation . Laron syndrome patients may have a lower incidence of some age-related conditions, but do not appear to live meaningfully longer than the rest of the human population. One of the most important lessons of the past thirty years of study of calorie restriction and growth hormone metabolism in the context of aging is that these interventions produce much larger effects in short-lived species than in long-lived species.

Nonetheless, disruption of growth hormone metabolism remains an active area of study. You might recall a paper published five years ago or so in which researchers showed that disruption of growth hormone metabolism starting in adult life , at six months of age in mice, still produced a slowing of aging. Here, the same team repeats the same effort starting at twelve months of age, mid-life for mice. The size of effect on life span is much the same in male mice when starting at this later age, but worse in female mice. In either case, the extension of life span is modest in comparison to life-long disruption of growth hormone metabolism, less than 10%. Like the existence of Laron syndrome, this argues against putting meaningful effort into attempts to build human therapies based on this mechanism.
Midlife Growth Hormone Receptor Ablation Extends Healthy Lifespan and Induces Sex-Specific Hepatic Transcriptional Changes at Single-Cell Resolution

Suppression of growth hormone (GH) signaling is known to be effective to extend lifespan in mammals, yet most models rely on congenital disruption of the GH/ insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) axis. Whether modulation of this pathway later in life can still influence aging and the underlying cellular mechanisms remains incompletely understood. To address this, we ablated the growth hormone receptor (Ghr) at 12-months of age in mice (12mGHRKO), using a tamoxifen-inducible model.

This midlife Ghr disruption produced the expected endocrine signature of GH resistance, including reduced circulating IGF-1 and elevated GH levels. Importantly, lifespan was significantly extended in both sexes without major effects on somatic growth. Despite increased adiposity , male 12mGHRKO mice exhibited improved insulin sensitivity and protection against age-related deterioration of neuromuscular performance and bone microarchitecture . Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) of liver tissue identified a reduction of B-cells in both sexes and a dimorphic transcriptional remodeling, including a shift toward feminized gene expression in male hepatocytes , marked by reduced male-biased gene expression and increased female-biased transcriptional programs, consistent with impaired pulsatile GH- STAT5 signaling.

Together, these findings demonstrate that suppression of GH signaling initiated in middle age is sufficient to reshape hepatic transcriptional programs and promote healthy longevity, supporting the GH/IGF-1 axis as a promising target for gerotherapeutic interventions.

articles.titleOriginal: Mattel Spotlights ‘Barbie in the Nutcracker’ with 25th Anniversary Celebration
articles.summaryOriginal: The rollout includes new dolls, Netflix specials, and more, celebrating the beloved film. The post Mattel Spotlights ‘Barbie in the Nutcracker’ with 25th Anniversary Celebration appeared first on The Toy Book .

bodyOriginal.text: In 2001, Barbie made her feature-length debut with Barbie in the Nutcracker , setting the stage for another two decades of animated Barbie adventures. As the film turns 25 this year, Mattel is celebrating with new toys, television specials, and more for fans of all ages.

Leading the celebration is an all-new Barbie in the Nutcracker television special. Coming to Netflix this November, the animated special puts a new spin on the beloved 2001 classic, this time casting Barbie “Malibu” as Clara and Barbie “Brooklyn” as the Sugar Plum Fairy. On their adventure to rescue Ken the Nutcracker, the friends will travel through a variety of enchanted lands, face off against the mischievous Rat King, and discover that if kids truly believe in themselves, magical things can happen.
Celebrate 25 years of 'Barbie in the Nutcracker' with a new television special. | Source: Mattel
The re-imagined 'Barbie in the Nutcracker' will air on Netflix this November. | Source: Mattel
Relive the magic of the original 2001 film. | Source: Mattel
Tim Curry returns as the voice of the Rat King's Father. | Source: Mattel
Discover the magic of friendship. | Source: Mattel

The ballet is also getting some more modern moves, thanks to dance legend Debbie Allen . As the special’s co-executive producer and choreographer, Allen created unique numbers that blend classical dance with today’s hip hop, all set to music by Macy Schmidt. The late Tim Curry also returns to the voice cast as the Rat King’s Father, the natural progression of his appearance as the Rat King in the original.

But families don’t have to wait until November to return to the Land of Sweets. The classic 2001 Barbie in the Nutcracker is now available to stream on Netflix, so parents who grew up with the original Clara and the Sugarplum Princess can share the magic of the film that kicked off more than two decades of animated adventures with a new generation of fans.
Barbie Nutcracker Clara and Sugar Plum Fairy 2-Pack. | Source: Mattel
Barbie Nutcracker Ballerina and Chelsea Snow Fairies. | Source: Mattel
Barbie Nutcracker Land of Sweets Horse and Sled. | Source: Mattel
Barbie Sugar Plum Fairy and Clara Deluxe Doll. | Source: Mattel

The anniversary celebration continues off-screen with a new Barbie in the Nutcracker toy collection. Available now at major retailers, kids can re-create the classic story with dolls inspired by Clara, Daisy, the Sugar Plum Fairy, Land of Sweets ballerinas, Chelsea Snow Fairies, and more, complete with poseable bodies that mimic real ballet positions. Each doll features a variety of enchanting accessories and outfits, and select toys can even magically transform their tutus with a twirl.

Nathan Baynard, Vice President and Head of Barbie, Mattel , said, “At Barbie, we’re proud to create stories that inspire imagination and spark joy across generations. As we celebrate the 25th anniversary of Barbie in the Nutcracker , this collection honors the enduring magic of dance and storytelling while inviting today’s families to create new holiday traditions and memories together.”

articles.summaryOriginal: The artist describes that he aims to make his paintings “feel like songs.” Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Art History and Pop Culture Converge in Friedrich Kunath’s ‘The Nearest Faraway Place’ appeared first on Colossal .

bodyOriginal.text: Friedrich Kunath describes that he aims to make his paintings “feel like songs.” The logo for the band Oasis turns up in a top corner of “Sometimes I’m Almost There,” and there is a kind of surreal, set-like quality to his vibrant, cinematic works. “Kunath explores themes of distance and (re)location, where a longing emerges between the place you’re in and the place you’re destined to be,” says a statement for his exhibition The Nearest Faraway Place, presented by Pace in Seoul.

The artist taps into art history with compositions redolent of the tradition of Weltlandschaft , or “the world landscape,” which can be traced to the Northern Renaissance. There’s also a strong nod to the Hudson River School , which drew on 19th-century European Romanticism. Kunath tips in references to pop culture, from the ubiquitous “The End” marking the finale of theatrical releases and phrases superimposed on uncanny situations, like the eponymous painting “The most beautiful world in the world” depicting an existential aerial advertisement.

bodyOriginal.alt: a painting by Frederich Kunath of a landscape with a large cloud at sunrise and the Oasis band logo in the top left corner

bodyOriginal.text: “Sometimes I’m Almost There” (2026), oil on canvas, 121.9 x 97.8 centimeters

Kunath is known for traversing realms of pop culture, irony, and fiction, often with a kind of nostalgic wistfulness and a tinge of the comedic. We’re initially drawn in to what appears like a traditional landscape, then quickly diverted by sticker-like additions of cartoonish, sometimes absurd characters.

As the basis of the artist’s works, romantic landscapes are already inherently invented; they may resemble real places, but the glistening light and idyllic absence of structures or people portray a kind of ideal. Kunath opens that door further. “By bringing together aesthetic contexts and familiar tropes, he materializes his subconscious,” the gallery says. “Feelings arise before we know where they come from.”
The Nearest Faraway Place continues through October 24. See more on Kunath’s Instagram .

articles.titleOriginal: Game Store Day Is Growing, and the Tabletop Community Is Ready to Play
articles.summaryOriginal: Excitement is building for Game Store Day as the tabletop industry comes together to celebrate local stores, welcome more players, and create memorable experiences on November 7. The post Game Store Day Is Growing, and the Tabletop Community Is Ready to Play appeared first on The Toy Book .

bodyOriginal.text: One big day to celebrate the places we play.

On Saturday, November 7, GAMA: The Tabletop Game Association will celebrate the second annual Game Store Day , bringing retailers, publishers, creators, and players together for a day dedicated to the Friendly Local Game Stores at the heart of tabletop gaming.
And if the industry’s response is any indication, year two is shaping up to be a good one.

Game Store Day is a free GAMA member-only initiative created to celebrate and elevate the role independent game stores play in their communities. Inspired by events like Record Store Day and Indie Bookstore Day, the annual celebration spotlights the creativity, diversity, and passion of tabletop gaming and the stores that bring it all together.

Local game stores do a lot more than put games on shelves. They’re where someone learns their first game, discovers their next favorite one, finds a regular gaming group, or sits down across the table from someone who might become a new friend.
Game Store Day gives those stores an opportunity to turn it up a notch.

“Game Store Day is a great excuse for a store to put their best foot forward and create magic and wonder in their space,” said Kylie of Games Unlimited in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. “Get creative with the experiences you offer, and you’ll have an event your customers will be talking about as they patiently look forward to next year.”

bodyOriginal.alt: Game Store Day 2026 Publishers | Source: GAMA

bodyOriginal.text: Game Store Day 2026 Publishers | Source: GAMA
That excitement isn’t limited to retailers.
Game Store Day is designed to bring the tabletop ecosystem together, with publishers, creators, media, retailers, and fans all playing a role in building excitement around local stores.
And publishers have answered the call in a big way.

GAMA has already doubled its publisher participation goal for 2026, bringing even more industry support behind this year’s celebration. Participating publishers are helping create opportunities for players and retailers to discover games, demos, promotional items, and other surprises as part of Game Store Day.
That growing participation is exactly what Game Store Day is about: giving the entire industry a reason to rally around the places where tabletop gaming happens every day.
For stores, that means November 7 is a chance to show off what makes their community special.

Host a tournament. Teach a new game. Break out a demo. Plan something unexpected. Introduce regular customers to something they’ve never played or give someone who’s never stepped inside a game store a reason to pull up a chair.
There isn’t one right way to celebrate Game Store Day. In fact, the best events look different everywhere you go.
RELATED WiT Stories: The Human Shelf: Why Connections Still Wins at Retail
With publisher participation already gaining momentum, it’s time for Friendly Local Game Stores to get involved.

Participating stores will join a coordinated campaign designed to drive foot traffic, increase visibility, and put local game stores at the center of tabletop excitement heading into the holiday season. Game Store Day builds on GAMA-led initiatives like Winter Wishlist by combining industry promotion with grassroots community participation to help players discover games and the local stores that carry them.

GAMA member retailers have until October 8 to register for Game Store Day 2026 and guarantee delivery of a Publisher’s Box. You can register up until Nov. 2 to receive a digital marketing Toolkit. The sooner the better!
So, start thinking about what November 7 could look like in your store. Get creative. Give your regulars something to look forward to. Give somebody a new reason to walk through the door.
And create a little magic while you’re at it.
Register your store and learn more about Game Store Day at gamestoreday.com .

articles.summaryOriginal: Trapezoidal motifs appear throughout this concrete condominium block in Tokyo, designed by Japanese studio Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture. According to Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture, the angular, trapezoidal motifs that feature throughout the design were informed by the project's

bodyOriginal.text: Trapezoidal motifs appear throughout this concrete condominium block in Tokyo , designed by Japanese studio Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture .
Named Shin Nakano Trapezoidal, the five-storey block of 11 residential units was designed for local developer Real Partners.

According to Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture , the angular, trapezoidal motifs that feature throughout the design were informed by the project's location on the Musashino Plateau, a large tableland in western Tokyo.

bodyOriginal.alt: Concrete housing block by Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture

bodyOriginal.text: Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture has completed a concrete condominium block in Tokyo "The Musashino Plateau is one of those landscapes that people live on without ever seeing," said principal architect Ryuichi Sasaki told Dezeen.
"Our challenge was to take something as abstract as a position within a plateau and translate it into a motif that residents encounter every day," he continued.
"[It is] in the facade they walk past, in the shadows on the stairs, in the light that reaches their rooms."

bodyOriginal.alt: Exterior view of Shin Nakano Trapezoidal condos

bodyOriginal.text: Trapezoidal motifs feature throughout the design On the block's eastern edge, a sheltered entrance area is framed by tall, trapezoidal concrete columns and features trapezoidal floor tiles.
A large sliding metal door leads into a lobby and stairwell, where an industrial-feeling steel staircase with grille treads allows daylight to filter through.
This lobby divides the block into three wings across which the apartments are separated, with a combination of single-storey and duplex units that extend into a basement and rooftop terrace.

bodyOriginal.alt: Interior view of condo at Shin Nakano Trapezoidal by Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture

bodyOriginal.text: The five-storey block contains 11 residential units Each apartment takes advantage of views over the street to the south and a park to the north, with large metal-framed windows that slide open for cross-ventilation.
The interiors are deliberately minimal and pared-back, with timber floors, exposed concrete ceilings, white-painted walls and large areas of built-in storage.

Read: Groupwork completes "world-first" high-rise held up by stone exoskeleton The trapezoidal motif was carried through into openings in the interior walls and floors, staircase balustrades and even the floor plan of some rooms.
Externally, the block is finished in exposed concrete, with textured trapezoidal and triangular panels created by embossing the surface of the concrete after it was poured.

bodyOriginal.alt: Condo interior by Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture

bodyOriginal.text: Their interiors have been kept minimal and pared-back "A residential building of this scale is experienced in fragments — an entrance, a stair, a window — so the motif had to work at every one of those moments," said Sasaki.
"We are proud to offer the residents of Nakano a building that connects them, quietly and daily, to the ground it stands on," he added.

bodyOriginal.alt: Bedroom interior at Shin Nakano Trapezoidal housing block in Tokyo

bodyOriginal.text: Each apartment has large metal-framed windows Previous projects by Ryuichi Sasaki Architecture include a mixed-use development containing homes and a community performance space in Tokyo, which was housed within similarly angular concrete volumes.
Elsewhere in Tokyo, Kenta Hirayama recently created the steel-clad House in Kinuta and Kenta Sano & Associates combined a glass-fronted dance studio with a house .
The photography is by Takumi Ota Photography .

articles.titleOriginal: Growth Hormone Receptor Antagonism Modestly Slows Aging in Mice
articles.summaryOriginal: Researchers here run a much larger than usual mouse study to show a ~10% slowing of aging, depending on how one slices the data, in mice genetically engineered to exhibit a growth hormone mutation that changes the interaction of circulating growth hormone with the growth hormone receptor on cell surfaces. Growth hormone is switched from a receptor agonist (binds with and activates the receptor) to

bodyOriginal.text: Researchers here run a much larger than usual mouse study to show a ~10% slowing of aging, depending on how one slices the data, in mice genetically engineered to exhibit a growth hormone mutation that changes the interaction of circulating growth hormone with the growth hormone receptor on cell surfaces. Growth hormone is switched from a receptor agonist (binds with and activates the receptor ) to a receptor antagonist (binds with the receptor without activating it, blocking other molecules from activating it). This extension of life is entirely expected given all of the long-lived mouse lineages in which growth hormone metabolism is in some way sabotaged . This specific form of sabotage had not been tested rigorously, however. While interesting, it is worth noting that humans with Laron syndrome , an inherited dysfunction of growth hormone metabolism analogous to many of the mouse models exhibiting longevity, do not appear to live meaningfully longer than the rest of the human population.

Interventions that disrupt growth hormone (GH) action are recognized as some of the most potent methods for extending lifespan. Accordingly, GH receptor antagonists (GHA) represent potential therapeutics to improve healthspan . Somavert ( Pegvisomant for injection), used for treating patients with acromegaly , is currently the only FDA approved GHA. This drug was based on our laboratory's early 1990s discovery that mutating a codon for a conserved glycine - at position 119 in bovine GH or 120 in human GH - to a variety of amino acids , including lysine , ultimately converted GH from an agonist to antagonist. Since Pegvisomant has poor affinity to rodent GHR, it has not been tested for its ability to extend lifespan in rodents.

To address this gap, we evaluated survival in GHA transgenic mice, a mouse line that played a crucial role in the discovery and development of Pegvisomant and has been maintained in our lab since 1991. While a prior study with several limitations failed to detect lifespan extension in GHA mice, our current study addressing these limitations shows that both median and maximal lifespan were significantly increased in male and female GHA mice, with maximal lifespan extended by 186 and 265 days, respectively. Analysis of an independent cohort of 2-year-old mice revealed that GHA males and females were less frail with enhanced grip strength despite increased adiposity . These findings demonstrate for the first time that GH antagonism can improve health and extend lifespan.

articles.titleOriginal: Studio Saar tops LDF pavilion with police and rain shields
articles.summaryOriginal: This year's London Design Festival landmark project, The Pangolin Shield, explores Britain and India's colonial history through a bamboo-grid pavilion covered with shields used both for protection and aggression. Named after, and baring a resemblance to, a pangolin – a scaly mammal – the pavilion is located on the newly pedestrianised part of The Strand The post Studio Saar tops LDF pavilion with

bodyOriginal.text: This year's London Design Festival landmark project, The Pangolin Shield, explores Britain and India's colonial history through a bamboo-grid pavilion covered with shields used both for protection and aggression.

Named after, and baring a resemblance to, a pangolin – a scaly mammal – the pavilion is located on the newly pedestrianised part of The Strand outside London's Somerset House and near India House . According to Studio Saar co-founder Ananya Singhal, this location had a significant impact on the project.
"The Strand is right next to Somerset House and right next to India House," Singhal told Dezeen.

"Somerset House is where the British Navy was administered from during the colonial period, and India House is where the Indian High Commission is," he continued. "So this site has a very interesting history behind the relationship between India and the UK."

bodyOriginal.alt: The Pangolin Shield,

bodyOriginal.text: Studio Saar designed The Pangolin Shield pavilion for LDF The Pangolin Shield pavilion also faces a bust of India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru.
To Singhal, placing the pavilion in this location was an opportunity to underline the new relationship that India has with the UK "and possibly the world", he said.
"We're an Indo-UK practice working with a British engineer, so there was something about this project and the site which kind of brought that combination together," Singhal said.

bodyOriginal.alt: Pavilion on The Strand in London

bodyOriginal.text: It is located on a pedestrianised part of The Strand The Pangolin Shield was designed by Studio Saar and structural engineers Atelier One , led by founder Neil Thomas. It was constructed using a bamboo grid shell, which the studios wanted to use because of the material's many positive characteristics.
"It's lightweight, it's durable, it grows very quickly; once you finish with it, it's biodegradable, and you can make super interesting shapes from it," Singhal said.

bodyOriginal.alt: Police shields on the roof of a pavilion

bodyOriginal.text: The roof is made from police shields The gridded shell structure that forms the base – and which is strengthened by steel fastenings – was then covered in two very different types of shields.
On top of the bamboo grid is a first layer, made from traditional Indian police shields constructed out of lathis, a type of bamboo stick.
This first layer is then covered by knups, woven rain shields that are traditionally used by farmers in the north-east of India.

Read: Studio Saar creates forest-like pavilion at Design Mumbai "The police shields were designed by the British colonial rulers to keep riots down in India all those years ago; it's really beautiful, the idea of making it a part of the structure that shelters both visitors and the locals here," Singhal said.
"The knups are from Meghalaya, the wettest place on Earth – it gets more than two metres of rain per year and its name literally means 'the land of the clouds'," he continued.

bodyOriginal.alt: Rain shields on a pavilion for LDF

bodyOriginal.text: On one side the police shields are covered in rain shields The design of the pavilion, which resembles a creature covered in scales, was also inspired by Singhal's work outside of Studio Saar.

"I'm a wildlife photographer and conservationist, and one of the animals that I hear about a lot is the pangolin, which is the most trafficked mammal on Earth," he explained. "So I wanted to create a structure that brought the pangolin into conversation."

bodyOriginal.alt: Small model of a pangolin

bodyOriginal.text: A model of a pangolin was placed inside the pavilion Inside the pavilion, visitors can admire a sculpture of the pangolin and look at the drawings for the project.
As the pavilion was damaged when it was transported from India to the UK, it will be shown with an interior scaffold during London Design Festival (LDF) due to "abundant caution," Singhal said.
"It's a public space and there are going to be drunk people coming up and down this street", he said in reference to the risk of the pavilion being damaged.

bodyOriginal.alt: Pavilion on the Strand in London

bodyOriginal.text: During LDF the pavilion will be supported with the addition of internal scaffolding Overall, Singhal believes that the project is a good representation of the values that Studio Saar stands for.
"Something which we really hold dear as a practice is the idea you can take small, humble, crafted things and combine them to make amazing things," he said.
"And that's the piece that we've practised in many areas, and what we would really love to do, and that's what we're doing here with the police shields and the knups."
Other projects on show at London Design Festival include Craft x Tech, which explores Japanese craft in a contemporary way, and Lozi's modular plywood furniture .

The Pangolin Shield is on show at The Strand, WC2 1HL, from 12 to 20 September. See our London Design Festival 2026 guide on Dezeen Events Guide for information about the many other exhibitions, installations and talks that take place during the week.
